Drought-Stricken Nevada Town Erupts Over Luxury Development’s Initiative for ‘Firefighter Pond’

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1416 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Should a private developer have the ability to build a human-made pond in the middle of a drought-stricken region?
  • That’s the question at the center of a growing debate in Clark County, NV, where water is scarce and locals are skeptical about a luxury development's plan to create a massive water feature.
  • Joel Laub and his partner, Randall Jones, began developing the Reserve at Red Rock Canyon in 2022, aiming to create a high-end luxury community amid the Nevada wilderness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Should a private developer have the ability to build a human-made pond in the middle of a drought-stricken region? What if that developer states that firefighters can access the pond to fight wildfires?

That’s the question at the center of a growing debate in Clark County, NV, where water is scarce and locals are skeptical about a luxury development's plan to create a massive water feature.

Joel Laub and his partner, Randall Jones, began developing the Reserve at Red Rock Canyon in 2022, aiming to create a high-end luxury community amid the Nevada wilderness. The Reserve is being built on 65 acres that were once home to the Bonnie Springs Ranch, a historic, Old West-themed family resort that once featured horseback riding and a small zoo.

Two-acre empty plots in the community start at $7.5 million. But that’s not what has the community up in arms. Instead, it’s what the Reserve is touting on its website: a large human-made pond in the middle of the property.

To outsiders, it seems like just one feature in a long list of amenities. But for some locals in Clark County, which was declared a natural disaster area due to drought earlier this year, the pond seems like a slap in the face—even as the developers attempt to position it as a fire safety "dip pond.".

“This little dip pond here is really fire safety as an afterthought, and I think that’s pretty obvious in terms of even their planning,” said Sarah J. McCrea-Dameron, a Blue Diamond, NV, resident and former deputy fire chief from Las Vegas Fire & Rescue, at a zoning commission meeting this past week. “It’s not in an area that’s necessary, and it’s not the best use of that water and that precious resource for our community.“.

It has been revealed that the Reserve at Red Rock Canyon development sits within the Red Rock Canyon Conservation Area, an expansive 195,000-acre area within the Mojave Desert. Aztec sandstone foundations dating back to 180 million years can be found in the area, along with sea fossils and hundreds of local bird species. More than 3 million people visit the area each year.

Water for the area is supplied by the Colorado River. In recent years, the river and the several lakes it feeds have been pushed to the limit, as fresh development, coupled with more frequent droughts, have strained resources.

The river doesn’t just supply necessary water to communities across the Southwest: It also produces much-needed hydropower for the region.

Earlier this year, Lake Powell, one of the lakes fed by the Colorado River, dropped to its lowest level in history, threatening to shut down the Glen Canyon Dam, which supplies power to Wyoming, Utah, Colorado, Fresh Mexico, Arizona, Nevada, and Nebraska.

Communities around the Red Rock Canyon Conservation Area take the mantle of water conservation seriously. In fact, in 2020, the nearby community of Blue Diamond issued a temporary moratorium on “the issuance of additional water commitments” that remains in place.

Now, as the developers Laub and Jones offer unbuilt lots in their newly introduced development for $7.5 million, they are pitching the proposed pond as a neighborhood amenity.

“Paths and roads will meander past water features fed by the canyon’s natural springs,” the development’s website states.

Sources indicate that but those types of features are typically prohibited by Clark County’s Title 30, which governs building and development in the area. Title 30 right now prohibits the creation of human-made lakes of any size and water features greater than 10 square feet of surface area. So the developers stressed that the human-made pond would be fed via private water rights, and therefore not impede on community resources. Instead of using Colorado River resources, the project would be fed using groundwater.

Bob Gronauer, the developers' lawyer, said the water feature would be a “dip pond”—a water source for use by firefighting helicopters. Wildfires are a frequent problem in the region. In 2025 alone, there were 619 fires in the state, which destroyed more than 368,000 acres.

In fact, the developers have already signed a use agreement with the Nevada Division of Forestry. The developers claimed the NDF came to them to ask them to create the pond, but the NDF stated the developers approached them about the partnership, the Nevada Independent reported.

Recent findings suggest that "We reached out to the Bureau of Land Management Red Rock management staff at the visitor center, Save Red Rock, Friends of Red Rock, as well as the Nature Conservancy Nevada immediately upon purchasing the property to work with them to make this development compatible with the Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area," Laub tells Realtor.com. (Laub is the chairman of the Nature Conservancy board.).

Laub claims the idea for the dip pond actually came from the BLM.

"They asked if we could work with them on fire management in Red Rock Canyon, and would we consider providing water for firefighting. Of course our answer was yes. We have a 220,000-gallon water tank designed into our water system for supplying water to our fire hydrants, and we agreed to provide a fire hydrant for the BLM water tankers to fill up in the event of a wildfire," Laub continues.

"The ponds are designed to fit into the canyon ecosystem and look natural but also to be compatible with helicopter firefighting.".

Laub tells Realtor.com that they've already been testing the wells in the canyon, and "none of the testing results from these wells has indicated a draw down of significance from our use of the water system.".

He also notes that they purchased the water rights from Bonnie Springs Ranch, which had been in use for more than 60 years.

"The property has had ponds, streams, pools, and springs from the original ranch in 1952," he explains.

To expedite the creation of the dip pools, the developers proposed an amendment to Title 30 that would add language permitting “a body of water, served from standalone private water rights, within 1,000 feet of a National Conservation Area, intended for fire suppression and life safety purposes as agreed upon with a State or Federal Agency.”In October, Clark County Planning Commission's professional staff recommended denying the amendment.

"As proposed, there is no indication of how these water features would be designed, the capacity of these water features, or other potential uses for the stored water. The proliferation of non-essential water features will place an additional burden on the existing water supply," the staff recommendation read. "Furthermore, this request may encourage additional non-essential water features within residential and nonresidential development.".

Recent findings suggest that however, the Planning Commission approved the amendment by a vote of 6-1. It then went to the Clark County Zoning Board for approval. On Wednesday night, during the public comment period of the meeting, around a dozen community members spoke out against the planned feature.

“You can design a decorative water feature and then call it a dip pond. You can offer to let the Forest Service use it knowing that they never will because of the way it’s designed and location, but that doesn’t make that decorative water feature a piece of critical fire infrastructure," noted former Clark County Fire Capt. Erik Klausen.

“They’re trying to put a plastic fire helmet on this water feature and tell us it’s about public safety,” he continued.

At the end of the public comment period, all seven commissioners voted in favor of the proposed amendment, though, as Commissioner Justin Jones noted, the approval of the amendment does not mean the dip pond project has been approved.

Furthermore, noted Commissioner Marilyn Kirkpatrick, the project needs to be fit for purpose.

"If it's a fire-suppression pond, then it has to be a fire-suppression pond in my mind," remarked Kirkpatrick. "It should stay as a fire-supression pond, not as a recreational venue, not as irrigation, because that water is supposed to be there for a reason.".

Realtor.com has reached out to developer Jones and lawyer Gronauer for comment.

  • As AI shifts from building models to running them every day, costly graphics processing unit racks and the liquid cooling they demand keep many companies renting compute instead.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Enterprises cannot own their own infrastructure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 14:29 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Power-efficient inference chips are becoming the entry price for enterprises that want to run AI on hardware they own.

As AI shifts from building models to running them every day, costly graphics processing unit racks and the liquid cooling they demand keep many companies renting compute instead. That gap is opening room for challengers to the incumbent chipmakers. Axelera AI B.V. built its business at the edge with low-power chips and edge AI development tools, and it is now taking that technology into data center infrastructure, according to Manuel Botija (pictured), vice president and head of product at Axelera.

Recent findings suggest that “Enterprises cannot own their own infrastructure. They’re locked out because of the cost and the power,” Botija noted. “We are enabling them now to own it. It’s not that we are helping the world save power or save money — which we are — but it’s that we are unlocking use cases that were simply not possible before.”.

Botija spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how power-efficient inference chips are heading for the data center and how enterprises locked out by the cost and power of GPU racks can own their own AI infrastructure instead of renting compute. (* Disclosure below.).

In a recent development, “Having a six-kilowatt server that can perform like a data centre GPU is a pretty big deal,” he said. “It basically means that they have some storage equipment, some networking equipment, some traditional CPU equipment, and next to all of that, they can also insert some AI inference hardware acceleration without needing to go and rebuild another server room or another data center.”.

Sources indicate that for enterprises that would rather own their AI hardware than pay a recurring cloud bill, the barriers have been steep. A GPU rack costs at least $1 million, often far more, and usually requires liquid cooling, Botija noted. Axelera’s answer rests on digital in-memory computing, a technique that grew out of its founders’ research and gives the tech giant’s power-efficient inference chips a performance-per-watt advantage.

“Now you can own your own infrastructure,” Botija noted. “You can amortize those investments and … reduce your opex, and therefore be more profitable as a firm.”.

#64899. Stopping statins after 70 may be safer than expected, but there's a catch

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1151 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Stopping statins after 70 may be safer than expected, but there's a catch

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1151 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A major fresh study suggests that many adults age 70 and older who have never experienced a heart attack or stroke may be able to stop taking statins without substantially increasing their short-term cardiovascular risks.
  • Industry observers note that the independent, preliminary research was presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, held November 6 through 9 in Chicago.
  • An estimated 25% of American adults have elevated levels of low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-C), commonly called "bad cholesterol." When too much LDL cholesterol accumulates in the arteries, it can restrict blood flow and contribute to heart attacks and strokes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A major fresh study suggests that many adults age 70 and older who have never experienced a heart attack or stroke may be able to stop taking statins without substantially increasing their short-term cardiovascular risks. However, the findings also point to a possible increase in risk over a longer period, making the decision more complicated than it initially appears.

Industry observers note that the independent, preliminary research was presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, held November 6 through 9 in Chicago. The annual conference brings together cardiovascular researchers and healthcare professionals from around the world to share scientific discoveries, emerging evidence, and advances in clinical care.

An estimated 25% of American adults have elevated levels of low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-C), commonly called "bad cholesterol." When too much LDL cholesterol accumulates in the arteries, it can restrict blood flow and contribute to heart attacks and strokes. Statins are widely prescribed to lower cholesterol and reduce these risks, including in people who have never experienced a cardiovascular event. This preventive approach remains a central part of the American Heart Association's 2026 joint guideline on dyslipidemia.

Do Older Adults Need to Keep Taking Statins?

Although statins are an established treatment for reducing cardiovascular risk, questions remain about how much benefit they provide when people reach their 70s and beyond, particularly if they have never had a heart attack or stroke.

Industry observers note that "While the Association's recent joint guideline recommends lifestyle and potentially medication for people with high LDL-C at younger ages to reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke, recent studies question the health benefits of continuing statins in the later decades of life," said study author Rita F. Redberg, M.D., M.Sc., FAHA, professor of cardiology and the Araxe Vilensky Endowed Chair in Cardiology at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine. "A few previous studies assessed the safety of discontinuing statins for primary prevention at age 70 and later, and they found no difference in mortality. One study suggested quality of life improvements after stopping statins. Whether it is safe to discontinue statins to prevent a first CVD event in the elderly remained unclear and the question we explored in our study.".

Industry observers note that to investigate, researchers enrolled nearly 1,900 adults aged 70 and older who were taking statins specifically to prevent a first cardiovascular event. Every participant also had at least two chronic medical conditions, such as a history of cancer or lung disease.

Sources indicate that participants were divided into two groups. One group stopped taking statins, while the other continued their prescribed treatment. Researchers tracked their health for approximately two years, with additional follow-up extending as long as four years. They examined rates of heart attack, stroke, and death, along with changes in quality of life, muscle pain, falls, and muscle wasting (known as sarcopenia).

What Happened When Older Adults Stopped Statins?

According to recent reports, the initial findings were largely reassuring. After approximately two years, participants who stopped taking statins did not experience a statistically significant increase in heart attacks, strokes, or deaths compared with those who remained on the medications.

Stopping treatment also did not produce measurable improvements in the other outcomes researchers examined. Quality of life, muscle discomfort, falls, and muscle wasting were similar in both groups.

According to recent reports, there was, however, a small difference in cardiovascular outcomes. Over the first two years, the results indicated approximately one additional cardiovascular event for every 40 people who discontinued statins compared with those who continued treatment.

The longer follow-up revealed a more concerning pattern. Over a period of up to four years, 12.7% of participants who stopped statins experienced a heart attack, stroke, or death, compared with 9.2% of those who kept taking the medications.

Longer Follow-Up Reveals a Potential Risk.

Redberg explained that the higher rate of serious outcomes during the four-year follow-up represents a new finding in research on statin discontinuation among older adults. She suggested that the difference may have emerged because this trial included more participants and tracked them for a longer period than earlier studies.

These results complicate the question of whether older adults should continue cholesterol treatment indefinitely. While the findings suggest that stopping statins may be a reasonable option for many people in this age group, they also indicate that remaining on treatment could offer some protection over time.

Sources indicate that "This small, increased risk of cardiovascular events means that one cannot make a general recommendation about stopping statins in this patient population," she said. "There should be shared decision-making between the patient and the healthcare professional to know if it is appropriate for an individual to discontinue the medication. In general, however, discontinuation is safe for most people who are in this age group and without a previous CVD event.".

Study Design and Key Limitations.

Industry observers note that the trial involved 1,880 participants aged 70 and older (average age of 77; 53% men, and 47% women), all of whom had at least two chronic health conditions. Individuals with established cardiovascular disease or a previous cardiovascular event were not eligible to participate.

Sources indicate that researchers conducted the study between November 2021 and April 2026 across 24 medical centers in Switzerland, France, and the Netherlands. Of the participants, 938 were assigned to discontinue statins, while 942 were assigned to continue taking their medications.

Throughout the trial and subsequent follow-up, researchers recorded heart attacks, acute ischemic strokes, and deaths from any cause. Participants also completed surveys assessing their overall quality of life, muscle pain, falls, and sarcopenia.

It has been revealed that one limitation was that some participants did not remain in their originally assigned groups. Some people instructed to stop statins eventually resumed treatment, while others assigned to continue taking statins stopped using them. Altogether, approximately 14% of participants switched from their assigned treatment approach during the study.

It has been revealed that to determine whether these changes affected the findings, the researchers performed several additional statistical analyses. The results remained unchanged.

Taken together, the findings suggest that discontinuing statins may be an option for many adults over 70 who have not previously experienced cardiovascular disease, especially when considering outcomes over the first two years. However, the higher rate of heart attacks, strokes, and deaths during longer follow-up underscores why stopping treatment should be an individualized decision made with a healthcare professional rather than a general recommendation for all older adults.

#64896. Industry News: Forcing yourself to smile can actually make you miserable

Industry News: Forcing yourself to smile can actually make you miserable

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1001 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A smile might brighten your mood, but new research suggests that forcing yourself to smile over and over can have the opposite effect.
  • In a recent development, for years, psychologist Nicholas Coles, Ph.D., studied evidence suggesting that even an artificial smile could make someone feel a little happier.
  • According to recent reports, "I used to work in customer service.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A smile might brighten your mood, but new research suggests that forcing yourself to smile over and over can have the opposite effect. When smiling becomes an obligation, especially one tied to financial pressure, it may actually leave people feeling less happy and more irritated.

In a recent development, for years, psychologist Nicholas Coles, Ph.D., studied evidence suggesting that even an artificial smile could make someone feel a little happier. Yet those findings never quite matched his own experiences.

According to recent reports, "I used to work in customer service. I actually got written up for my inability to keep smiling at work at an unnamed theme park in Florida," laughed Coles, a professor of psychology at the University of Florida. "So I'm looking at all this evidence I had accrued so far that smiling boosts happiness and realizing it flies in the face of my own experiences in the world.".

That contradiction inspired Coles and his colleagues to investigate what happens when people must keep smiling, rather than simply trying it once. Their findings suggest an important distinction: A brief, intentional smile can provide a small emotional lift, but repeatedly putting on a smile under pressure can undermine happiness.

Testing How Forced Smiling Affects Happiness.

Recent findings suggest that to explore this difference, Coles worked with researchers Annabel Dang and Joao Francisco Goes Braga Takayanagi to design an experiment that more closely resembled the demands of customer service jobs. Their findings were published on October 1 in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology.

In a recent development, "We tried to combine the classic way of studying it in a lab with some extra ingredients that we might see in the real world. We told participants that we would pay them less if they weren't successfully smiling," Coles noted. "We also controlled the number of times they have to do it, because in customer service, every interaction is another faked smile.".

In a recent development, the online experiment initially enrolled 1,201 people, with data from 1,174 included in the final analysis. Participants were shown images designed to produce different emotional reactions. Some depicted appealing subjects, such as kittens and flowers, while others showed disturbing situations, including theft and mistreatment of animals.

Sources indicate that during the experiment, participants either deliberately formed a smile or allowed their facial expressions to develop naturally. Depending on their assigned group, they completed the exercise once or repeated it 10 times.

Industry observers note that to introduce an element of pressure, researchers warned half the participants that failing to follow the smiling instructions could cost them $2 from their $6 payment. However, nobody actually lost any money, and every participant received the full amount.

When Fake Smiles Start to Backfire.

According to recent reports, after completing each task, participants reported how happy they felt. The results indicated that the emotional effects of smiling depended on how often people had to do it and whether they felt pressured.

When participants viewed unpleasant images, producing a single smile gave their mood a modest boost. This benefit appeared even among those who had been warned about a possible financial penalty. However, the positive effect weakened when smiling was repeated, and it disappeared when repeated smiles were combined with the threat of losing money.

The pattern was even more revealing when people looked at pleasant pictures. Smiling just once offered little additional happiness compared with allowing their faces to respond naturally. But when participants had to smile repeatedly or felt pressure to do so, their happiness ratings actually fell below those of people who responded naturally.

It has been revealed that further analysis revealed another unexpected consequence. In the pleasant picture conditions, forced smiling was also associated with increased irritation and anger.

"If you only force a smile once without any financial penalties, you can see the improvement in happiness. So what psychologists were seeing in their lab is right," he remarked. "But when you make it a little bit more like the real world, where you have to keep repeating it, and if you don't do it well, you get financial penalties, you see it completely reverse.".

The Hidden Emotional Cost of Smiling at Work.

These findings may help explain why expectations to appear cheerful throughout the workday can become frustrating rather than uplifting.

Industry observers note that the issue has already sparked controversy in the workplace. In recent years, Target faced widespread criticism over a policy requiring employees to smile when customers came within a specified distance. Although the policy was intended to encourage friendly interactions, Coles argues that such requirements can interfere with people's ability to express their emotions naturally.

The problem may extend beyond employees. Customers can also feel obligated to respond positively to friendliness that is being imposed rather than offered spontaneously. According to Coles, these expectations limit the emotional freedom of both sides of the interaction.

Could Trying Less to Be Happy Make Us Happier?

After spending years investigating how people can improve their emotional well-being, Coles has begun considering a broader question. Rather than constantly searching for ways to increase happiness, might people be better off placing greater value on simply being content?

His research suggests that efforts to manufacture positive emotions do not always produce the intended results. Sometimes, trying too hard to appear happy can make the experience less pleasant.

"As a society, we have placed such an immense amount of emphasis on trying to make ourselves feel happier than we at the moment are," he noted, "much less emphasis on just being content with what we have.".

Recent findings suggest that bitcoin price is getting hammered in the aftermath of the FOMC minutes. Gold isn’t doing much better; oil and stocks have joined the sell-off. The markets are already nervous about the Federal Reserve’s next decision, and yesterday’s FOMC minutes gave us another reason to worry: policymakers are still talking about raising interest rates.

In a recent development, almost all officials saw further hikes as appropriate under their baseline outlook. Two even floated the possibility of a bigger increase if inflation refuses to cool.

This is a nasty combination for markets. Bitcoin fell around 3.2% over 24 hours, gold futures dropped more than 3%, and WTI crude lost around 3%. The dollar climbed to a 19-month high. Wall Street was mixed, though, with the Nasdaq finishing higher while the Dow and S&P 500 slipped.

Here’s the comparison. In March 2020, the Fed was slashing rates, buying bonds and throwing emergency liquidity at a financial system under immense pressure. Congress approved a $2.2 trillion rescue package to keep households and businesses afloat.

Today, we are watching markets fall while the Fed is possibly making money more expensive.

In a recent development, october’s FOMC minutes weren’t exactly what markets wanted to hear. The Fed held rates at 3.75%–4% during its October meeting, but almost all participants believed further increases would likely be appropriate. Two officials also noted a hike larger than the usual 25 basis points could be considered if inflation data came in hotter than expected.

And there was more in those minutes than just interest rates. Officials raised concerns about hedge fund leverage and the growing debt tied to artificial intelligence investments. Some financing arrangements could become a problem if investors start questioning enormous AI spending, and whether it will generate the returns companies expect.

Recent findings suggest that the risk is forced selling. Leveraged funds facing losses or investor withdrawals may have to dump assets swiftly, potentially pushing prices down further.

Gold has its own problem. A stronger dollar and higher interest rates make it less attractive to investors who can earn a return elsewhere. Bitcoin price, meanwhile, remains vulnerable when traders cut exposure to speculative assets.

Sources indicate that the Fed hasn’t declared a financial emergency. Its minutes actually describe the banking system as resilient. But officials are clearly paying attention to risks that could amplify a market shock.

Discover: The Best Token Presales.

March 2020 was brutal. COVID-19 lockdowns brought businesses to a standstill. Investors rushed for cash, stocks collapsed, and Bitcoin briefly slipped below $4,000 after sitting near $10,000 just weeks earlier.

The Federal Reserve didn’t wait around. It cut rates by 50 basis points on March 3, then delivered another 100-basis-point cut on March 15. The federal funds target range dropped to 0%–0.25%.

On March 23, the Fed unveiled unlimited purchases of Treasury securities and mortgage-backed securities, promising to buy whatever amounts were necessary to support market functioning. It also introduced emergency lending programmes to keep credit flowing.

Sources indicate that president Donald Trump signed the $2.2 trillion CARES Act on March 27. The package included direct payments to eligible Americans, expanded unemployment benefits, and assistance for businesses struggling to survive lockdowns. The Paycheck Protection Program gave small businesses access to loans designed to help them keep employees on payroll.

The response was enormous, but the economy was facing an extraordinary shutdown. Millions of Americans had lost their jobs, businesses were closing, and normal economic activity had practically disappeared.

Recent findings suggest that markets eventually bounced back. The S&P 500 recovered its pre-pandemic record by August 2020. Bitcoin climbed above $12,000 during the same month.

The current US economy isn’t in the same position as it was during the pandemic. Inflation remains above the Fed’s 2% target, and policymakers are discussing rate increases rather than cuts.

Recent findings suggest that slashing rates to zero and flooding markets with liquidity might help asset prices. It could also make inflation worse. Another multitrillion-dollar spending package would face an entirely different argument in Congress, especially without a pandemic-style economic shutdown.

According to recent reports, the Fed doesn’t have to choose between doing nothing and repeating the 2020 rescue. If banks struggle to fund themselves or credit markets start freezing, it can step in with emergency lending and liquidity operations. That’s a much narrower response than another round of unlimited bond purchases.

In a recent development, the Fed’s concerns about leveraged hedge funds and AI financing could become more relevant if investors start selling indiscriminately. A market correction is one thing. Forced selling spreading through the financial system is another.

At the moment, there’s no evidence that we’re facing another March 2020. The banking system remains resilient, and falling Bitcoin prices alone won’t trigger a government bailout.

Sources indicate that but the Fed has a problem that didn’t exist in quite the same way during the pandemic. It may need to protect financial stability without giving up its fight against inflation. In 2020, Washington opened the taps. This time, we wait and see, and Bitcoin price will survive.

Traveling Home for Thanksgiving? How Smart Buyers Turn Holiday Visits Into Neighborhood Recon

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (650 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • That’s why it’s no surprise that the latest Migration Trends report by the National Association of Realtors® found that 30% of buyers who relocated did so to be near family.
  • Whether the goal is to care for aging parents, assist with childcare, or simply enjoy more time with loved ones, living near family can make a positive difference in everyday life.
  • If you’ve been contemplating buying a home closer to family, your Thanksgiving visit could be the perfect opportunity to start exploring what life in a newly introduced area could look like.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For most people, family is everything.

That’s why it’s no surprise that the latest Migration Trends report by the National Association of Realtors® found that 30% of buyers who relocated did so to be near family.

Whether the goal is to care for aging parents, assist with childcare, or simply enjoy more time with loved ones, living near family can make a positive difference in everyday life.

If you’ve been contemplating buying a home closer to family, your Thanksgiving visit could be the perfect opportunity to start exploring what life in a newly introduced area could look like.

Since you’re already making the trip, it only makes sense to get a firsthand look at the neighborhoods, homes, and local amenities to help you determine whether the move is worthwhile for your budget and lifestyle.

According to recent reports, “Seeing how a community operates when people are home, traffic is heavier, and daily routines are stressed can help you make an informed decision about where to plant roots,” notes Cameron Walker, real estate expert and manager of the agent network at Clever Real Estate in St. Louis.

Once you arrive in town for Thanksgiving, take a commute during rush hour.

Then, walk around the area during the day and at night and check out local shops, restaurants, parks, and other attractions.

“Be sure to speak to locals about traffic, parking, safety, noise, and other concerns that might arise during different seasons,” indicates Walker.

Pay attention to all the small details that will matter if you make the move: sidewalk length and quality, road conditions, street parking availability, cell service reliability, distance to the nearest airport, and proximity to hospitals.

If you have time, you may also want to attend a few open houses and meet with a real estate agent.

Industry observers note that “Look at homes for sale, recent home sales, and the length of time homes are taking to sell, as well as how many price reductions are being made. Learn about local property taxes, insurance costs, and whether there are many homes for sale that fit your price range,” Walker adds.

In addition, focus on schools, childcare, commute times, and other amenities to make sure you’d feel comfortable with your daily routines.

In the late fall and early winter, typical buyer activity drops off sharply in many markets. That’s why it’s a great time to look for a home.

Depending on the market, it may open the doors to some unique negotiation leverage.

“As fewer and fewer buyers are ‘in the market’ from Thanksgiving to the Latest Year, sellers may become more flexible in their terms,” says Sander Scott, owner and broker of Net Real Estate in Traverse City, MI.

And there may be even more opportunities this year.

According to the Realtor.com® October 2026 housing report, approximately 1 in 5 listings had a price reduction, while active inventory was up 7.4% compared to last year.

That means you might have more housing options at your disposal and sellers may be more willing to adjust their asking prices.

“Focus on the right location and daily function. After all, saving money on a house that makes the childcare or caregiving goal harder to achieve defeats the purpose,” Scott adds.

In addition, think of a refinance as a potential bonus—not your initiative.

Sources indicate that “Rates come and go, but the purchase price is forever. Always consider the purchase price, the monthly payment, and whether you can afford it in the long run,” explains Walker.

Look beyond the monthly mortgage payment and understand the total cost of ownership. Being close to family is no fun if it forces you to become house poor as a result.

“Thanksgiving is about catching up with family members and eating turkey, but it may also be about seeing if a relocation is feasible for your particular financial situation,” Walker adds.

Breaking: Exercise after ACL surgery may protect knees from early osteoarthritis

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A serious knee injury can cause problems that persist long after surgery, but fresh research suggests that the right exercise program could make a major difference.
  • Sources indicate that recovery from ACL surgery is often more difficult than expected.
  • Medical guidelines recommend combining exercise rehabilitation with patient education after ACL surgery, yet many people receive treatment that falls short of these recommendations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A serious knee injury can cause problems that persist long after surgery, but fresh research suggests that the right exercise program could make a major difference. A clinical trial led by researchers at La Trobe University found that supervised exercise and education can improve knee health, reduce pain, and enhance quality of life in young adults recovering from anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. The findings also offer hope for addressing their elevated risk of developing knee osteoarthritis at an unusually young age.

Sources indicate that recovery from ACL surgery is often more difficult than expected. About half of patients are still dissatisfied with their knee health two years after the procedure. Even more concerning, roughly half develop signs of early-onset knee osteoarthritis within a decade, often before reaching age 40.

Medical guidelines recommend combining exercise rehabilitation with patient education after ACL surgery, yet many people receive treatment that falls short of these recommendations. One obstacle is the widespread concern, shared by some patients and healthcare professionals, that exercise could damage already vulnerable knee cartilage.

A New Approach to Recovery After ACL Surgery.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate whether additional rehabilitation could help, researchers at La Trobe University's Sport and Exercise Medicine Research Centre conducted the SUPER-Knee clinical trial. It was the first study to evaluate the benefits of combining exercise therapy and education more than nine months after ACL reconstruction, a time when patients are generally expected to have recovered even though many continue to experience problems.

The researchers enrolled 184 adults between the ages of 18 and 40 who were still struggling with knee symptoms one to three years after their operations. Participants were assigned to either a progressive exercise therapy program or a comparison group that received a single educational session.

The findings, published in Annals of Internal Medicine, indicated that participants who completed the four-month program under the guidance of a physical therapist experienced improvements in knee health and muscle strength, along with less pain and better quality of life.

Industry observers note that importantly, these benefits came without evidence that the exercises were damaging knee cartilage or worsening early osteoarthritis. The results challenge the belief that physical activity necessarily makes injured knees worse.

Exercise Offers Hope Against Early Knee Osteoarthritis.

Associate Professor Adam Culvenor, who led the research, remarked the findings provide much-needed evidence about how to help younger patients who remain at risk of knee osteoarthritis following ACL surgery.

Sources indicate that "At the moment we don't have any high-quality evidence for what treatments should be offered to young people at risk of early-onset knee osteoarthritis. Our SUPER-Knee study changes this, and addresses a globally recognized research priority," Associate Professor Culvenor mentioned.

"Our study showed physiotherapist-supervised exercise therapy and education is safe and should be recommended to improve the knee health of young people at high risk of early-onset osteoarthritis following ACL reconstruction.

"The evidence generated by the SUPER-Knee trial can be used to enhancement international clinical practice guidelines for rehabilitation following ACL reconstruction and could be a lifeline for young people struggling after serious knee injuries.

"The intervention is ready to be used by local health professionals with minimal specialized equipment or staff training.".

According to recent reports, the findings could influence how clinicians approach rehabilitation long after ACL surgery, particularly for patients whose symptoms continue beyond the usual recovery period. Although the trial did not establish whether the program prevents osteoarthritis over the long term, it demonstrated that supervised exercise can improve knee health without accelerating the cartilage damage or early osteoarthritis researchers were monitoring.

Years of Knee Pain After a Serious Sports Injury.

It has been revealed that for Ruby Cumming, the challenges of recovering from ACL surgery were deeply personal. In 2019, when she was 24, she tore her ACL while playing Australian rules football. Hoping to return to the sport as quickly as possible, she underwent reconstructive surgery within six weeks.

Sources indicate that but the operation did not lead to the recovery she had imagined. Her rehabilitation continued for years, and she ultimately decided not to return to football.

"I thought if I had the surgery and did the rehab I'd be able to get back to normal. After surgery impacted my entire life - not just footy - I changed my outlook and decided I wanted to avoid re-injuring my knee ever again so haven't played contact sport since," Ruby noted.

"Experiencing regular pain, not being able to walk, getting public transport to work and living independently all became really challenging for me.".

Cumming remained committed to her rehabilitation, regularly attending physical therapy appointments and performing prescribed exercises. She initially exercised daily before moving to a weekly routine. Despite those efforts, she continued to experience varying degrees of knee pain every day for three to four years.

Her experience changed after she enrolled in the SUPER-Knee trial and began participating in weekly rehabilitation sessions supervised by a physical therapist.

"When I joined the SUPER-Knee program and did weekly physio-supervised rehab, this improved my pain significantly," Ruby said.

In a recent development, the research suggests that people who continue to struggle after ACL reconstruction may benefit from additional structured rehabilitation, even years after their original injury. Because the program requires little specialized equipment or additional staff training, researchers say healthcare professionals could readily incorporate it into existing treatment services.

The SUPER-Knee clinical trial received funding through a Project Grant from Australia's National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC).

#64890. What we learned from Nvidia’s first earnings call without Jensen Huang

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2904 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

What we learned from Nvidia’s first earnings call without Jensen Huang

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2904 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, nvidia Corp.
  • Industry observers note that revenue more than doubled year-over-year.
  • According to recent reports, this was Nvidia’s first earnings call without co-founder Jensen Huang, whose resignation as president and chief executive was announced on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 14:32 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala.

According to recent reports, nvidia Corp. reported its quarterly results this week, and contrary to the prevailing narrative, the sky didn’t fall.

Industry observers note that revenue more than doubled year-over-year. The Vera Rubin chip platform achieved the fastest product ramp in the company’s history, and management raised its fiscal 2028 growth outlook to roughly 75%, up from 70%. By all accounts, it was a solid beat and raise.

According to recent reports, this was Nvidia’s first earnings call without co-founder Jensen Huang, whose resignation as president and chief executive was announced on Nov. 12. Board Chair Harvey Jones told investors that the resignation followed the “disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the tech giant’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.” Hours after Huang publicly said he would be willing to return, Jones said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and would not take questions about the circumstances or the board’s ongoing investigation.

Colette Kress, the longtime chief financial officer who is now also serving as interim CEO, set the tone in her first minute: “Our ambition will not change. Our passion for innovation will not change, and our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change.”.

After listening to the call, I believe Nvidia answered the short-term question and left the long-term one open. The firm made a convincing case that it can execute without its founder. It has yet to show who decides where it goes next. Here are five things we learned and what they mean for those who buy, budget for or operate artificial intelligence infrastructure.

The fear going into the call was disruption. The quarter closed before Huang’s exit, so the results can’t settle that. The guidance can, and it went up. Hyperscalers brought Vera Rubin into production in about a month, half the time Grace Blackwell required. The roadmap is set through Vera Rubin Ultra next year and Feynman in 2028, and Kress mentioned the supply agreements extend through the end of the decade.

She explained that the past month has been “Business as usual.” Kress added, “We’ve engaged with our customers, suppliers and partners. They’re all 100% behind us.” She also noted that TSMC leadership was at Nvidia’s offices this week.

Industry observers note that I have long held that Nvidia’s moat was never the silicon. It’s the accumulated layers of systems, software and supply chain built around it. The past week was the first real test of that view, and so far, it’s holding. A yearly product cadence this complex runs on thousands of engineers and a supply chain planned years in advance.

Asked about talent retention, Kress acknowledged that “there are diverse opinions” among employees while insisting they are “committed to doing their life’s work” at Nvidia. The company’s talent can’t be overstated, and although Huang was the face of the company, the employees are what made it tick.

Sources indicate that earlier this week, Cisco Systems Inc. CEO Chuck Robbins appeared with Brian Sozzi. When asked whether he still trusts Nvidia, Robbins replied immediately, “Absolutely.” He added, “The industry’s bigger than one person. I don’t care how good you are. There are a lot of smart people. There are 42,000 people at Nvidia. So I’m not all that concerned.” Huang may have been the most visible Nvidia employee, but the company is full of smart, driven people. Leadership understands this, and I expect turnover to have minimal impact.

Employee retention is a top-of-mind issue for Nvidia executives. Business Insider reported this week that the organization held its first all-hands meeting after Huang. The article noted that Kress declared looks to accelerate pay raises and equity grants, Jones discussed the CEO search and Buck outlined the roadmap. It’s reasonable to believe that Huang’s departure was a shock to employees, but the business goes on, and I expect things to settle down in short order.

It has been revealed that for information technology buyers, nothing changes about what you’ve ordered or planned over the next 18 to 24 months. Don’t pause a deployment because of a leadership headline. The advice I gave in August still applies: Welcome Nvidia’s simplification and hedge the dependency.

Sources indicate that one of the more interesting comments on the call came from Jones, not Kress. In describing the CEO search, which will consider both internal and external candidates, he mentioned the board “appreciates that we’re living in a world where advanced silicon technologies and national security dynamics are driving major changes in our marketplace. Our newly introduced CEO will need to navigate those waters carefully.”.

In a recent development, that was paired with immediate action. On the morning of earnings, the board created a standing national security and export control oversight committee of three directors that will retain outside experts. Kress disclosed that Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China and noted that the U.S. Commerce Department issued upcoming export controls this week, which the firm “still has some time to study.”.

Industry observers note that huang was a product visionary who also served as the industry’s chief diplomat. The board is now signaling that fluency in Washington is a core requirement, on par with technical vision.

Industry observers note that for IT leaders at multinationals, export policy is now a deployment variable. The upcoming Commerce rule is intended to block remote access to advanced chips via data centers in third countries, so the location of your capacity and who can access it are now compliance questions. Bring your compliance team into AI infrastructure planning early.

It has been revealed that with demand still far ahead of supply, who gets Nvidia systems matters more than what they cost. Kress laid out the criteria more clearly than I’ve heard before. First are land, power and shell, meaning whether a customer’s facility is ready to receive and use the gear in the quarter it ships. Second is capital. Third, for customers that aren’t investment-grade, is proof of off-take, or evidence that someone has committed to use the capacity.

Recent findings suggest that “All are getting the same pricing,” Kress said. “That is super important for us, and we just need to assure that they are ready on their side in terms of being able to accept the compute.”.

Recent findings suggest that those same factors were incorporated into the guidance. Kress remarked the outlook “considers data center readiness, the strength and durability of end customer demand, and our customers’ access to capital.” The reality is that the AI bottleneck has shifted from the chip to the building, the grid and the balance sheet. Nvidia is serving as the industry’s underwriter, determining who is ready.

Recent findings suggest that the lesson for enterprise buyers is that readiness is the currency. If you want on-premises systems, secure power, cooling and funding before requesting allocation. If you can’t, buy capacity from a provider that has already cleared this hurdle. In my view, this also helps explain why sovereign AI is growing so rapidly for Nvidia. Those projects often arrive with land and power already in place.

Over the past year, Nvidia has used its balance sheet to seed the ecosystem through guarantees, investments, and commitments to neoclouds and AI labs. Though  neoclouds remain important, Kress brought a different tone to this audience. She said Nvidia will “continue to be disciplined and selective” in supporting neoclouds and that it is “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees” as other sources of capital become available. Asked about vendor financing, she acknowledged that “a lot of things have changed over this last quarter.”.

Two notable details emerged during the call. When Bernstein Research analyst Stacy Rasgon pressed on what he read as new disclosure language about neocloud commitments, Kress explained that Nvidia’s guarantees take effect only after a partner has raised its own debt and equity, built the facility and installed the compute. If the project stalls, the guarantee lapses.

Industry observers note that “Is it newly introduced? No. Did we change anything? No,” she said. Even so, spelling it out clarifies Nvidia’s participation in neoclouds. When asked about uses of capital beyond the share buyback, which she said Nvidia still plans to complete, she put suppliers first: “The top priority is going to be our suppliers.” Prepayments to expand capacity come before customer financing, which will be reserved for “very strong customers.”.

This was a critical piece of information for investors. I’ve previously compared vendor-financed neoclouds to the CLECs of the internet era, where the financing organization was left holding the bag. A CFO-led Nvidia appears to see the same risk. The result is a shakeout in which well-capitalized neoclouds with contracted demand grow stronger, while thinly funded ones struggle to secure systems. This should offer some comfort to investors that circular financing has been de-risked.

The flip side is that someone still must fund the buildout outside the hyperscalers. Kress pointed to infrastructure capital partners establishing financing platforms. Whether that money arrives as fast as Nvidia steps back is what to watch for.

My advice to IT buyers is to ask, before signing a multiyear deal with a neocloud, how it’s financed, how much capacity is committed and where it stands in Nvidia’s allocation queue. Those were niche questions a year ago. They should be standard due diligence now.

The demand story has shifted from training models to running agents, broadening what customers need from Nvidia. Citing OpenRouter data, Kress said agentic workloads now account for roughly 80% of tokens. Falling token prices are driving more usage, keeping GPU rental rates climbing.

According to recent reports, the CPU growth story shouldn’t surprise anyone. In May, I wrote that agentic AI opens a massive upcoming spigot for Nvidia on the CPU side. This quarter, demand outpaced supply. “Agentic AI is driving extraordinary demand for CPUs, far outstripping supply,” Kress said, noting that Nvidia’s Vera CPU is now adopted by CoreWeave, Meta, Nscale and Open AI. Agents spend much of their time calling tools, running code and moving data, which is general-purpose work. A CPU shortage amid a GPU boom shows how swiftly the workload is changing.

Nvidia is also filling in the layers above and around the hardware. The agent safety platform pairs OpenShell, which limits what agents can access, with Sentry, which runs on BlueField data processing units and monitors agent behavior in silicon. In my view, the biggest barrier to deploying agents in production is control, not model quality.

The network is part of this, too. Kress said co-packaged optics is in volume production, and Lambda’s deployment, announced at this week’s SC26 conference, is the first large-scale proof point. Nvidia is a formidable networking vendor, though buyers mixing accelerators will still want to weigh a network supplier that isn’t also selling a competing chip.

For IT buyers, proposal CPU capacity for agent workloads now, and insist that agent controls reside outside the model, in infrastructure you can audit.

The question of who the new CEO will be might not be just about Nvidia but about the entire industry. If the board goes internal, Ian Buck seems to be the frontrunner. Externally, the names most bandied about are Advanced Micro Devices Inc. CEO Lisa Su, Arm Ltd. CEO Rene Haas and Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian, or we could see Manuvir Das make a comeback and return to the company.

Most industry watchers describe Nvidia as a chip manufacturer, a view that is about a decade out of date. Nvidia’s value comes from the full systems it has built around its silicon. Each is a stack tailored to an industry: hardware, libraries, frameworks, pretrained models, simulation and developer tools, all tuned to work together.

The next CEO must treat silicon as a key layer of an open, secure, agentic enterprise stack. Enterprises won’t buy GPUs. They’ll buy outcomes: agents that run safely on governed data across clouds, on-premises and at the edge. Whoever runs Nvidia next must sell that outcome, play well within an ecosystem Nvidia doesn’t fully control, and make security a core part of the platform. Here are three dark-horse candidates to consider:.

Matt Garman. The Amazon Web Services Inc. CEO has led the world’s largest cloud through the shift to AI. He knows what it takes to turn infrastructure into consumable services at enormous scale. Garman also lives the open-stack approach: AWS offers model choice, runs its own Trainium chips alongside Nvidia’s, and sells to enterprises that want flexibility rather than lock-in. He would bring operational discipline and a deep feel for the customer. The question is whether Nvidia’s biggest customer-turned-competitor can credibly lead the supplier.

Jeetu Patel, Cisco Systems Inc.’s president and chief product officer, is the best storyteller in enterprise tech after Huang himself. He has spent the past few years rebuilding Cisco’s portfolio around secure AI infrastructure, integrating networking, security and observability into a single platform. That is exactly the “open, secure, agentic” stack Nvidia must deliver. Patel thinks in platforms, moves rapidly,and has been personally using AI agents to shape his product views. He also has deep enterprise credibility, which Nvidia needs more than additional credibility with hyperscalers.

Charlie Giancarlo, CEO of Everpure (formerly Pure Storage), may be the most underrated name here. He built networking businesses at Cisco, spent time in private equity, and has repositioned Pure as a data management firm. Storage revenue is growing thanks to hyperscaler wins. Giancarlo understands that agentic AI depends on data and that the data layer and the network are where enterprise AI succeeds or fails. He is a systems thinker who has led a platform transition before.

Two final points on the CEO hire: For some reason, there is a tremendous amount of industry chatter that Jensen Huang was the only person at Nvidia with key relationships with suppliers, partners, and other ecosystem providers. I know for a fact that is not true. Nvidia’s leadership, which includes Buck, Deb Shoquist (executive vice president of operations), Nico Caprez (vice president of global AI development), Gilad Shainer and Kevin Deierling (networking leadership), Kress and others, all have deep relationships with the ecosystem.

In a recent development, also, I wouldn’t expect the board to make a snap decision about its next CEO. The roadmap is baked beyond Feynman, and the company can continue for a couple of years, if needed. This is an important hire; the board should take its time and ensure it’s the right person.

Industry observers note that this call confirmed what many industry watchers, including me, have long believed: The moat was built in layers, and those layers held. Supply is constrained, the roadmap is set and customers are still asking for more than Nvidia can build.

Kress closed the call by saying, “We’ve got this.” On execution, I believe her. Kress is a steady hand right now, and the discipline she brings to capital allocation should make the AI buildout healthier. The bets that created Nvidia’s position, though, were placed years before the market arrived. Post-Jensen, Nvidia will continue to perform as it did; as Robbins put it, no one is bigger than the industry.

According to recent reports, my advice to IT buyers is to stick with current prepares and closely monitor the CEO search. Since Nvidia’s roadmap is baked through Feynman and beyond, it can ride momentum for the next two years or longer.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, for some children, learning math is much more difficult than it is for their classmates.
  • Recent findings suggest that one possible explanation lies in differences in how the brain selects and manages strategies for solving problems.
  • Industry observers note that the findings, published in JNeurosci, come from research led by Oliver Lasnick and colleagues at Stanford University.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for some children, learning math is much more difficult than it is for their classmates. Even when they practice and receive instruction, they may continue to struggle with problems that other children their age can solve more easily. Researchers are now uncovering clues about why these difficulties persist, and the answers may involve more than an understanding of numbers.

Recent findings suggest that one possible explanation lies in differences in how the brain selects and manages strategies for solving problems. A fresh study from Stanford University suggests that children with persistent math difficulties may have trouble adjusting their approach when faced with different mathematical challenges. The researchers also identified distinctive patterns of brain activity associated with these struggles.

Industry observers note that the findings, published in JNeurosci, come from research led by Oliver Lasnick and colleagues at Stanford University. Their work focused on children with a condition that causes ongoing difficulty with mathematical problem solving (developmental dyscalculia). Although the condition has been recognized for years, scientists are still working to understand the specific thinking processes and brain mechanisms that contribute to it.

Why Some Children Struggle With Math Strategies.

According to recent reports, to investigate these challenges, the Stanford team studied 68 children between the ages of 8 and 10. They examined how the children approached math problems, how effectively they used different strategies, and how their brain activity related to their performance.

Industry observers note that solving a math problem often requires more than knowing numbers or remembering arithmetic facts. Children must also decide which approach will work best. For example, a child might count individual numbers to find an answer or use a more efficient method based on a familiar mathematical relationship. As problems become more difficult, the ability to recognize when a different strategy is needed can become increasingly key.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers found that children with developmental dyscalculia were generally less effective at using different mathematical strategies than children without the condition. They took longer to shift from one method to another and were less responsive when the difficulty of a problem changed.

Another important difference involved learning to choose better strategies over time. While other children became more effective at selecting appropriate approaches, those with developmental dyscalculia did not show the same improvement. This suggests that their difficulties may involve not only performing calculations but also deciding how to approach a problem in the first place.

Brain Activity Reveals New Clues to Math Difficulties.

The researchers also examined patterns of brain activity to better understand what might be happening behind these behavioral differences.

They discovered that activity within a particular brain system differed between children with developmental dyscalculia and those who were more skilled at selecting and using math strategies. These neural patterns were not simply unrelated differences. They could also predict how effectively children counted and how well they switched between approaches when solving problems.

The findings highlight the possible importance of several mental abilities that extend beyond mathematics itself. These include attention, memory, and cognitive flexibility, which is the ability to adjust thinking or behavior when circumstances change.

Such abilities are part of what researchers often call executive functions. These mental processes help people organize information, stay focused on a task, hold relevant details in mind, and change plans when an approach is not working. In mathematics, they can help a child keep track of numbers, compare possible solutions, and recognize when to try a different method.

The Stanford findings suggest that difficulties involving these processes may contribute to the development of dyscalculia. Differences in brain activity may also help explain why some children have persistent trouble choosing and changing problem-solving strategies.

However, the observed connections do not establish that the brain activity differences directly cause the condition. They provide fresh evidence about the cognitive and neural processes associated with these mathematical difficulties.

Understanding Why Math Struggles Differ Between Children.

It has been revealed that an notable conclusion is that developmental dyscalculia does not appear to involve one simple problem shared by every affected child. Instead, different children may experience difficulties involving several interacting mental processes.

As Lasnick explains, "Importantly, this study also emphasizes the individual variability observed in dyscalculia, further demonstrating that the disorder reflects cognitive and neural dysfunction across multiple processes.".

By connecting children's mathematical behavior with measurable differences in brain activity, the research offers a more detailed picture of why math can be persistently challenging for some students.

According to recent reports, the findings also point toward the importance of looking beyond whether a child gets the correct answer. Understanding how children choose strategies, adapt to more difficult problems, and manage the mental demands of mathematics could ultimately help researchers develop better ways to identify and support those with developmental dyscalculia.

Melania Trump has given another look into her life as first lady with the premiere of “Melania: The Series,” a two-episode follow-up to the previously released "Melania" documentary.

Both the film and the series detail the weeks leading up to President Donald Trump’s January 2025 inauguration.

It has been revealed that in the first episode, which was released on Nov. 20, Melania prepares to resume her White House duties for a second term.

Sources indicate that “The role of the first lady is managing of the White House,” she explained. “And I think people don’t realize that the first lady is in charge of the residence.”.

She spoke at length about her approach to the role, noting the pride she takes in carrying out duties such as decorating the Washington, DC, landmark and planning events.

“I’m proud to elevate America through every detail brought to life within the White House,” said Melania. “Each event is carefully planned for months with the design, decor, cuisine, music, and atmosphere, all arranged with precision to showcase our nation’s beauty, strength, and grace.”.

Melania explained that her hope is for “the White House to showcase the greatness of American culture,” and that she wanted to elevate it “to the highest standard.”.

“We preserve. We restore. We build newly introduced stuff,” she said. “The White House should be the best of the best. It represents our country.”.

On Nov. 6, the president declared the Oval Office a national monument in an attempt to prevent future presidents from making changes to the renovations that have been made in his second term.

Industry observers note that “We’ve had tremendous victory in this office,” he remarked. “So we’re making it a national monument, and it will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape.”.

The White House has undergone extensive work since Trump has reentered office, including an overhaul of the iconic Rose Garden and a destruction of the East Wing to accommodate proposed plans for a 90,000-square-foot ballroom.

The first lady explained that she’s always had an interest in interior design, and when asked what kind of career she might have pursued had she not began working as a model before meeting her now-husband.

“I would continue studying architecture. I think I would do something with design,” she remarked. Melania had briefly attended the University of Ljubljana in Slovenia, where she studied the design discipline before leaving after a few months to pursue modeling.

She also revealed that she had prepares to bring some of her own pieces back to the White House.

“I will make it a home again,” she mentioned. “Last time was very beautiful, very comfortable. We all loved it, and we will do it again.”.

At one point, an off-screen interviewer notes that “so much thought” goes into each minute decision and asks Melania, “Does your husband recognize the detail?”.

It has been revealed that “He takes the whole experience in. He’s busy with his own job, and his mind’s going nonstop,” she said. “He has so much to take care of. So maybe he doesn’t realize how much work it is.”.

At another moment in the documentary, Melania hinted at the scope of her role, saying, “I know what my husband is doing and what my son is doing, but I don’t think they know what I’m doing.”.

Ahead of the inauguration, CNN reported that Melania would most likely not reside in the White House full time, which she appeared to confirm in the docuseries.

Recent findings suggest that “My home is in three cities. Each has purpose and serves varying parts of my life,” she said. “To balance this lifestyle, I’m very intentional and detail-oriented.”.

Aside from the White House, the Melania splits her time between Trump Tower in New York City and Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, FL.

She also expressed how much she values privacy, noting the importance of getting enough sleep and seeking “solitude.”.

Sources indicate that “I don’t need to be all the time with people,” remarked Melania. “I’m very happy in my own company. I always was.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Moving can be a time-consuming process, but it doesn't need to be stressful. We have some tips to help you enjoy a smooth move from your old home to the new. With the right system in place, there is no need to be overwhelmed by the move.

Before you make the move, check out these 5 packing tips.

Sources indicate that A common mistake people make when moving is to pack all of their belongings and move them, only to realize upon unpacking that many of the items should have been donated, sold, or thrown out. Before you pack, ruthlessly declutter your home. Packing things only to get rid of them at the latest house is a waste of your time and money.

Some questions to ask yourself as you declutter before packing are:.

As you pack and move, things are bound to get misplaced. To avoid the stress of a missing document or essential information, keep a folder (either physical, digital, or both) where you won't misplace it that is filled with essential paperwork. This might include:.

According to recent reports, greg Dallaire - Green Bay Real Estate Expert states, "Be sure to set up any utilities in the latest place to be turned on and ready when you arrive. Even if it means paying for utilities at two places for a brief overlap, it is often worth the convenience. In addition to basics like water and power, call ahead to make sure you will have internet, TV, and any other services you need.".

This is also a great time to move additional services to the new address, like security, pest control, or house cleaning.

Industry observers note that even if you are moving all in one day from one Calgary home to another, don't count on being able to unpack everything you need on night one. Instead, pack a suitcase with a few days' worth of clothes and necessities for everyone in the house. This way, you can settle into your newly introduced home without scrambling to find a towel or toothbrush before spending your first night there.

Industry observers note that the suitcase should include more than just your change of clothes and toiletries. Anything you might need for 2-3 days should be packed in it, including:.

In a recent development, as you pack, or have your movers pack, label each box with not just the contents inside but the room it should be placed in at the newly introduced home. This way, whether you have professional movers, a team of friends and family, or just your own household, it will be easy to make sure each box lands in the proper place.

One of the easiest ways to do this is by color coding. Assign a color to each room and label accordingly. For example, let's say the kitchen is blue. All boxes that should be brought to the kitchen will be labeled with blue tape, and on move-in day you can hang a large blue paper in the kitchen. This simple system will make unpacking much smoother.
